title: The silk-cotton tree
hookLine: the silk-cotton tree is tall and straight, but its fruit is tasteless and its leaves useless (Asa di Var, ang 470)

cards: In parts of North India and Punjab, there's a tree that's hard to miss when it blooms. Its branches are bare, and then suddenly they're covered in huge red flowers, so bright they look painted on.
It stands tall and straight, often taller than everything around it. In Punjabi it's the simmal. In English, the silk-cotton tree, for the fluffy cotton in its pods.
People in Guru Nanak's world knew it well, and he used it to open yesterday's salok, as a picture of a certain kind of life.

teach.b: Here's the salok's opening on ang 470, in paraphrase. The simmal tree is straight as an arrow, very tall and very thick.
But the birds that come to it full of hope go away disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers sickly, and its leaves are of no use. That's the whole picture, and it's sharp.
From a distance, the tree has everything: height, straightness, a trunk you can't get your arms around, a blaze of color. A bird flying over would think: there's my meal, there's my shade.
It lands, and finds nothing to eat, no shade worth sitting in. The tree isn't wicked. It just isn't useful.
Right after the tree come the lines we heard yesterday: mitthat neevee are the essence of virtue; the side of the scale that bends low is the heavy one. So the tree is the opposite of the scale.
All height and no weight. All show and no fruit. The salok keeps going, too.
It describes the guilty one who bows twice as low, the way a hunter crouches to stalk a deer. Low, but not humble. Then it asks: what's the use of bowing the head if the heart stays impure?
Put together, the lesson is about what people come to us for. Someone in trouble doesn't need us to be impressive.
They need fruit: a meal, a kind word, real shade.
The salok measures a life by what it gives, not how tall it stands.

how: Sikhs hear the salok of the simmal tree in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and teachers use it to describe a life that looks impressive but gives nothing.

o: a sacred tree planted at gurdwaras
a fruit tree that feeds the birds

games.q: the tree and the scale — tap the pairs.
p: bows low, but not in humility

s: in the salok, the simmal tree is short and crooked
it is straight, very tall and very thick, and still gives nothing.
the tree opens the same salok as sweetness and humility
the tree comes first, then mitthat neevee and the scale.
the salok praises anyone who bows low
it pictures a hunter bowing to stalk a deer, and asks what bowing is worth with an impure heart.

games.q: you're a bird, tired and hungry, and you see the tallest, brightest tree around. what happens when you land?
o: you find sweet fruit and deep shade.
you find nothing to eat and leave disappointed.
the tree is too tall to reach.
games.why: the birds come to the simmal full of hope and go away disappointed: its fruit is tasteless and its leaves useless.

practice: Picture the people who might come to you this week hoping for something, a coworker, a child, a neighbor, and ask what fruit each would actually need: time, help, a listening ear, not a performance.
Choose one small fruit you could give, and hold that picture for a few breaths. If you pray, say Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Simmal, the silk-cotton tree: tall, straight and bright, but the birds that come to it in hope leave with nothing.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: simmal, the silk-cotton tree, tall and red-flowered, common across Punjab.

carryVoice: Your line: useful, not tall. Fruit feeds; height only looks good. Day five hundred fifty-two, done.
